title: Welcome to Charting Waterloo Region!
text:
My brother and I with our family’s first Mercury Montego, circa 1974.
As a kid, one of my favourite family activities was “going for a drive.” That is literally what we called it. Mom or Dad would announce that we were “going for a drive” and the five of us would pile into the Montego and go for a drive. A drive never had a destination, unless we ended up in Hespeler, where we’d get ice cream cones at a convenience store on Cooper Street. Almost all of them meandered through one or more of the Region’s townships. I particularly liked it when Dad drove through the Paradise Lake area in Wellesley Township. I thought it was neat that we had a little cottage-y area so close to home. These drives gave me an early appreciation for the Region’s vastness and variety, and for the contrasts between its rock ‘n’ roll heart and its country soul. In CWR’s inaugural post, we’ll start exploring some of these contrasts and, in the process, answer the burning question: “What do the townships have more of, cows or people?”

title: Welcome to Charting Waterloo Region!
section: An urban island in a sea of farmland
text:
An urban island in a sea of farmland
If you haven’t gone for many drives through the townships, you may have no idea how vast they are compared to the cities in the Region’s heart. On a map, they look like a giant jaw chomping the urban core they nearly surround. Collectively, the townships cover 1,056 square km, or 77% of the Region’s 1,370 square km. Even the smallest township, North Dumfries, is considerably larger than Kitchener, the biggest city.

title: Welcome to Charting Waterloo Region!
text:
More cows than people?!
You don’t have to drive through the townships to guess that they have fewer people than the cities, but do they have fewer people than cows? Before we answer that, let’s see how many more people live in the cities than in the townships.
The latest estimates from 2025 show that, with 323,917 residents, Kitchener has by far the highest population in the Region, slightly more than the other two cities combined. Together, the cities have 631,721 people, or 89% of the Region’s population of 711,457. So despite covering 77% of the Region’s territory, the townships are home to only 79,736 residents, or 11% of total population. With a combined density of only 75 residents per square km, they certainly have lots of room for cows!
   
By the way, cows did not figure in this post when I conceived it. Not until I saw the density data did I jokingly add the “More cows than people?!” heading to this section. And even after that, it took a while before I thought, I wonder if there actually is any data on how many cows there are in the townships. Serendipitously, I found that not only is there a Census of Population, there’s also a Census of Agriculture, which most non-farmers have probably never heard of. And when I dug into the most recent data from 2021, I was excited to learn that I could answer the question, “What do the townships have more of, cows or people?”
(In case there are any cattle farmers reading, I do know that cows are a specific type of cattle, along with heifers, steers, bulls, and calves. But to this lifelong city dweller, they are all cows, so when I say cows, I mean cattle.)
The population estimates above are for 2025, but the cow data is from 2021, so for a fair comparison, we’ll use the 2021 census populations as well. On census day in 2021, just over 70,000 people lived in the townships. How many cows lived in them on that day? Click the other tab to find out.

PeoplePeople and cows


   


   



And there we have it: more cows than people lived in the townships on census day in 2021. What I thought was a joke turns out to be true!

title: Welcome to Charting Waterloo Region!
text:
What have we learned?
In CWR’s debut post, we learned that my family thought it was fun to jump in our gas-guzzling Mercury and aimlessly roam the rural roads through the Region’s rolling hills. We learned there were lots of roads and hills to roam because the townships cover 1,056 square km, over three-quarters of the Region’s 1,370 square km, while holding only 79,736 people, a ninth of its 711,457 residents. And last, we learned that with so much space and so few residents, the townships were home to more cows than people in 2021. In future posts, we’ll explore more differences between the cities and their country cousins. And if CWR is still active a year or so from now, when this year’s census data is released, we’ll revisit this post and see if cows still outnumber people in cattle country.

title: About
text:
ChartingWaterloo Region
    Learning about life in Waterloo Region, one chart at a time.

title: About
text:
What is it?
Charting Waterloo Region (CWR) is a local blog cobbled together to tell stories about life in Waterloo Region using data from (mostly) open sources. In snapshots—posts with a few charts and some basic analysis that can be read in under five minutes—and the occasional deep dive containing more rigorous analysis, CWR will answer questions from the fundamental to the frivolous. Has crime in the Region gotten worse over the past 25 years? CWR will take a stab at answering that (sorry!). What do the townships have more of, cows or people? CWR will investigate that burning issue as well. Basically, CWR is one guy’s effort to illustrate facts and features of Waterloo Region using well-designed charts built from open data.

title: About
text:
Who writes it?
The “one guy” in question is Greg Berberich. I’m a retired GenXer who was a Chartered Accountant for 30 years (I no longer hold the CA designation), the last 25 of those spent between UW and WLU earning a PhD in accounting, teaching, and doing institutional research. In case it’s not obvious, I really like playing with numbers, so as boring as it may sound to most people, that’s what I spend a lot of time doing. Except for a few years in Vancouver in the mid-90s, I’ve lived in the Region my whole life, the first 25 in Kitchener and since 1997 in Waterloo. CWR is my first blog and is basically me doing a hobby in public.

title: About
text:
Why does it exist?
After years (no kidding!) of procrastination, I’ve decided to start publishing some of my charts and analysis because I have learned a lot of interesting and sometimes startling things from them, so I figure it’s worth sharing some of what I learn with other Region residents who want to know more about where they live. And to my knowledge, aside from Jeff Outhit, who does some excellent data journalism for The Record, there is no local outlet that regularly visualizes data about the Region. CWR exists to help fill this gap.

title: About
section: Where does its data come from?
text:
Where does its data come from?
CWR relies primarily on Statistics Canada tables and government open-data portals for its data, supplemented by data from other sources, most of them publicly available. The “Data sources and reliability” section at the end of each post lists the sources, with their links and licences, where applicable. Notes about data reliability that are critical to the proper interpretation of chart data will also be included in this section.

title: About
text:
Is it independent?
My area of expertise as an accountant was in auditing. An auditor’s most-critical asset is their independence because without it, their opinion is worthless. I therefore take CWR’s independence very seriously. CWR is not funded by or affiliated with any government, public-service body, institution, or any other organization or person that could compromise its independence. All editorial decisions and opinions are mine alone.

title: About
text:
Does it have guiding principles?
Yes. Because I’m sharing charts and analysis with the public, I believe I have an obligation to earn readers’ trust, so CWR operates with a few key principles. I’ve read a literal shelf-load of books on data visualization. One called How Charts Lie by data journalist Alberto Cairo sets out several useful charting principles. I’ve adapted a few to guide CWR:

Charts will be based on reliable data.
Charts will not intentionally mislead and will aim not to mislead by accident.
Charts rarely serve as convincing arguments on their own, so they will be supplemented by honest, insightful analysis.
Charts show only what they show, so accompanying analysis will strive not to overstate their implications. Readers should do the same.
Charts will enhance our understanding of their subject matter and start conversations, not stop them.

CWR will also be free of pies and donuts. I love eating them, but they are bad for your charts.

title: About
text:
How is it built?
I use R, a popular language for doing data science, to produce CWR’s charts and tables, and to prepare the data behind them. Quarto combines the R code with my writing and renders it into the HTML, CSS, and images needed to produce the CWR website. These website elements get pushed to a GitHub folder and then served to you via GitHub Pages.
GoatCounter counts page views and post likes so I know which posts people find interesting. The site sets no cookies and records nothing that identifies you, so there is nothing to opt out of.

title: About
text:
Does it use AI?
Yes, I use Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, primarily as the supplier of the code used to modify the site’s infrastructure, to extract and transform the data, and to create the charts, although I do a lot of data-related coding myself (it’s fun!).
I make all editorial and design decisions, from the look and features of the site to the questions I answer, the analysis I do, and the charts I use, sometimes with Claude as a consultant. Claude also assists with background research, helping me identify sources, summarize lengthy documents, and synthesize content to provide useful context for my own analysis. I audit what Claude produces to ensure it’s relevant and reliable.
I write the analysis and discussion in each post, including the chart titles and subtitles, with Claude serving as a copy editor to help me clean up and refine the post for publication. Every statistic in a post’s text and every data point in its charts is taken from the data by code, and all of that code is public (see next section), so you can check any of it for accuracy. Claude drafts the charts’ alt text for screen readers, the Sources sections, each post’s README, and the data dictionary, then I review and edit them before posting. I take full responsibility for the final product and credit all sources used to produce it.

title: About
text:
Is it reproducible?
Yes, if you are so inclined, you can reproduce every post using the code and data in its associated GitHub folder. If you just want a post’s data, you can download a zip file containing the tables in CSV and Parquet formats, as well as an Excel workbook (when the tables are small enough), and a brief data dictionary describing the fields in each table. The “Reproducibility and data download” section at the end of each post contains links to the post’s GitHub folder and zipped data files.

title: About
text:
Can its content be reused?
Yes, everything on CWR is reusable, apart from material quoted from other sources, which stays under its owner’s terms. The text and charts are published under CC BY 4.0, so they can be copied, shared, or republished, including in the news, as long as CWR receives credit. And all the code is MIT licensed, so it can be reused as well. All data stays under the terms set by whoever published it.

title: About
text:
Could it contain mistakes?
Yes, I am human and can make mistakes. If you spot an error or have a question about the data, email me with the details. I will correct any post containing verified errors and add a dated note at the top of the post saying what changed.

title: About
section: Why doesn’t it have social-platform buttons or comments?
text:
Why doesn’t it have social-platform buttons or comments?
Social-platform buttons load code from those platforms that lets them track readers, which is inconsistent with CWR’s privacy practices. The site and each post have a Share button offering a copy-able link or a pre-filled email, so it’s easy to share CWR content without loading any trackers. CWR has no accounts on any platform, and none are planned. And comments require moderation, which is too much effort for what is essentially a hobby blog.

title: About
section: How often will it contain new content?
text:
How often will it contain new content?
While I gain my bearings as a blogger, I’m going to under-promise and hopefully over-deliver. My initial aim is to publish two Snapshots and one Deep dive a month. Once I optimize my workflow and get used to writing for a general audience, I’ll likely up it to one Snapshot a week but keep it to a single Deep dive per month.

title: About
text:
Can I subscribe to it?
If you use an RSS reader, which aggregates articles from sites you like into a handy chronological feed, CWR’s feed is at https://chartingwaterlooregion.ca/index.xml. Your reader will also find it if you just give it chartingwaterlooregion.ca. If enough people start reading this blog and indicate they’d like another way to subscribe, I will consider wiring that feature into the site.

title: About
text:
How does it make money?
It doesn’t. Like Neil Young, it’s sponsored by nobody. CWR is a non-commercial venture, so it doesn’t have ads and it won’t ask you to pay for a subscription. If you find a post enlightening, hit the Like button or drop me an email. That’s all the reward I need.
